title: Theory of Mind and Emergent Coordination

questions.question: What distinction does `run_trial(..., tom=...)` test?
options: Both policies choose the same fixed box, but ToM uses a larger grid.
ToM agents communicate by sending arbitrary messages while zeroth-order agents use a central planner.
Zeroth-order agents choose among remaining boxes without modeling peers; first-order ToM agents avoid boxes they infer peers are targeting.
Zeroth-order agents run a verifier, while ToM agents ignore observations.
questions.explanation: The `Agent.choose_target` branches on `tom`: false chooses uniformly from available boxes, true filters boxes inferred from recent observations when possible.

questions.question: What does `World.new(3)` initialize?
options: Three empty boxes and no tokens.
A 4×4 grid copied from the MARL lesson.
Two boxes with one token selected at random.
A world with `n_boxes=3` and tokens in boxes `{0, 1, 2}`.
questions.explanation: `World.new` returns `World(n_boxes=n, boxes_with_tokens=set(range(n)))`, so all three numbered boxes initially contain a token.

questions.question: How does a first-order ToM agent choose among boxes after observing peers?
options: It removes recently observed target boxes from the candidate list when alternatives remain, then samples.
It selects the box with the largest integer label.
It always follows the oldest observation, even if that box is gone.
It waits until another agent explicitly sends a completion message.
questions.explanation: The ToM branch builds `last_turn_targets`, filters `available` into `options`, and chooses from options if nonempty; otherwise it falls back to an available box.

questions.question: What does `run_trial` return for one seed?
options: Only a boolean indicating whether all agents finished.
A tuple of completed agents, collision duplications, and turns used.
The number of messages and the number of model calls.
The final world state and the random generator.
questions.explanation: The function returns `(completions, duplications, turns)`, which `bench` aggregates into full-completion counts, average duplications, and average turns.

questions.question: What is the role of the preference prime in the ToM trials?
options: It forces every agent to target box 0, creating a baseline collision.
It removes all tokens before the first turn.
It gives ToM agents observations of other agents' preferred boxes; zeroth-order agents ignore this extra information.
It lets zeroth-order agents inspect future random choices.
questions.explanation: When `tom` is true, each agent observes the others' `j % n_boxes` preference before the loop. The false branch does not use those observations.

questions.question: If two agents commit to the same box in a turn, how does the environment resolve it?
options: Both collect the token and the duplication counter stays zero.
The trial immediately fails without counting a turn.
The box is removed and all colliding agents are marked collected.
The first commitment in dictionary order collects; later commitments to that box waste the turn.
questions.explanation: The code counts `n - 1` duplications for a box, then uses a `taken` set so only the first commitment can discard that token and mark its agent collected.
